title: Job’s answer; the pilot in storm and calm; every human calamity
english: … recounted, and then she brings in her shameless counsel. And she does not even say to him openly, “Blaspheme.” For those who give wicked counsel do not dare to bring their counsel in uncovered. What are you saying, woman? When you ought to appease him, when you ought to reconcile him, do you advise him rather to provoke him? For if God did these things, one must entreat him, not blaspheme him. And how is it plain that I shall die even [if I speak]? But see what the woman thought about blasphemy: she supposed it able to bring death on the spot.

“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil?” (Job 2:10). For this blessed man, struck from every side, stood all the more firmly, and though he took countless arrows, he did not give way. He emptied the devil's quiver, but he himself did not fall, nor was he tripped up. Like the best of pilots, he was neither sunk when the sea raged and the waves rose up, nor did he grow careless when it was calm; in both kinds of season alike he kept his skill the same. Wealth did not puff him up, nor did poverty humble him. When affairs ran with the current, he did not lie back at his ease; and when nearly his whole household was overturned and utter ruin came, he was not thrown into confusion and did not disgrace his own courage.

Let the rich listen, let the poor listen. The account is useful to both, and the story profits everyone, those who prosper and those in calamity. For the champion of godliness, the crowned victor of the whole world, handled both kinds of weapons and set up his trophy in both; and when that demon came at him with every kind of warfare, he drew up his line against all of it and was proclaimed victor in all. Like a noble soldier who knows how to fight by night, to fight at walls, on foot and at sea, to shoot the bow and brandish the spear, and with slings and javelins and every manner of battle to overcome the enemy and win everywhere, so that noble man bore every trial with great courage: the trial from poverty, from hunger, from disease, from pain, from the loss of his children, from his friends, from his enemies, from his wife, from his servants. There was no human calamity that was not poured out on his body. Yet he rose above all the nets and climbed higher than the devil's fowling reeds.

And what is more wonderful still: everything came on him, everything beyond measure, and everything at once. Do not look only at this, that he suffered so much; add that it came not little by little, nor at intervals, but all together and at once. And this is no small addition to the trials. Among other men, first of all, no one would be found who has endured everything together. If a man wrestles with poverty, he still enjoys health. If he has been pierced through by poverty and disease both, he has often had a wife to console him in his troubles and to be a harbour for him. If he did not have such a wife, at least he had not been given such ruinous advice. If he had, at least he did not lose all his children at once. If he did lose them at once, at least not by such a kind of death. If even by such a death, still he had friends to comfort him. If he had none to comfort him, at least none trampled on him like this. If they did trample on him, at least his servants did not reproach him. If they reproached him, at least they did not spit in his face. If they spat in his face, at least he was not pierced through by such a disease, but had a room and a roof, and did not sit on the dung heap. If he did sit on the dung heap, at least he had people to hold out a hand to him. If he had no one to hold out a hand, at least he had no one trampling on him. But this man endured all of it.

“They came to him, each from his own country: Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Baldad sovereign of the Sauchaeans, Sophar king of the Minaeans” (Job 2:11). Your presence is friendly, and friendly is the advice. Eliphaz: “God has scattered me,” or “contempt of my God.” Teman: “their failing.” Sophar: “watchman,” or “contempt.” Baldad: “growing old,” and “glorious.” Sauchaeans: “their idle talk.”

“When his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, they came to him, each from his own country” (Job 2:11). title: Friends delayed; seven days’ watch; Job’s pain without blasphemy
english: … strangeness of the calamity seemed beyond belief too: that Job was really sitting on a dung heap with no one to help him. And they waited to confirm the report through more people, or else to send someone and see whether what was being said was true. In these things, then, the time was spent. Besides this, once they learned the truth, being kings and about to travel abroad, they had first to set the affairs of their houses in good order and to put others in their own place over their subjects. All this kept them busy, and they were delayed. And unless they had been men very much beloved and righteous, they would not have left their own countries and kingdoms and come to visit; they would have met the need through others.

One may also consider that the putting off of their arrival was a kind of divine dispensation. For since the whole contest was brought to its end together with the friends' dialogue, when God gave his answer and restored and crowned the righteous man, a divine dispensation came about: the friends were delayed so that the disease might be drawn out, and the righteous man, having contended the more, might be proclaimed by God the more justly.

“And they came to him with one accord, to comfort him and to visit him” (Job 2:11). Symmachus rendered it this way: “For they agreed together to come to share his suffering and to console him.” See from this too that still more time passed, until, sending messages to one another, they arranged their meeting in one place and their arrival. “And they sprinkled earth on their heads” (Job 2:12). “They sat beside him seven days and seven nights” (Job 2:13).

Scripture did not say that they sat beside him seven days from morning to evening, nor seven nights from evening to morning. It is plain, then, that they sat with him most of the day and withdrew to see to their necessary needs; then they came back again and sat with him far into the night, and going away once more, they came to him again at dawn. That is the mark of the truest and most sympathetic friends. But Scripture, following common usage, said it in this way without qualification: “They sat beside him seven days and seven nights.” For when it says too that Jacob served fourteen years and was burned by the heat of the day and the frost of the night (Genesis 31:40-41), did he then never go under a roof? Did he get no rest at all in the whole of that time? To split hairs over these things is mere chatter; for, as I said, Scripture uses common usage. But since some mock Scripture and tear it apart as false on this ground too (“How,” they say, “could they have gone on without food and without sleep for so many days?”), we have been forced to be dragged into their untimely pettiness.

But with these things the second main part has been completed. Making a preliminary survey of the third, we say that the righteous man does feel pain, and no one would deny it; for virtue does not belong to those who feel nothing, but to those who live wisely in the midst of their sufferings. [He is in anguish]: outwardly, he is stung most sharply by the blow in his flesh; inwardly, as a righteous and God-loving man, he sees some people scandalized at the sufferings, as though the glory of God were being torn apart in his case if the righteous man endures these things. For when he says, “Why have you set me up as one who pleads against you?” (Job 7:20), he himself was not pleading against God, far from it! For to whom could he make his plea? But this is what he means: “Why, Master, is your name blasphemed because of me?” And he is no less troubled and dizzy with fear that he may have suffered a fuller abandonment by God. For nothing punishes a God-loving soul so much as suspecting that it has been forsaken by God; it would choose death ten thousand times rather than be left among the living with pains and such a suspicion.

At the loss of his possessions and the sudden death of his children we have heard what words of thanksgiving he uttered, and how he corrected his wife when she had thought something unfitting about the Master, and what he said after the trial, the contempt and the sharp suffering, and how none of the mishaps that befall human beings threw him into confusion. But when the friends arrived, righteous and sympathetic men, he thought it the right moment, seeing their patience and their love, to speak and to make public the pains of his soul; and in the literal sense what he says carries no danger. For the devil had a single aim: to bring the righteous man to blaspheme God. But he clearly never did this; rather he spoke well of God and sent up words of thanksgiving. title: Job opens his mouth; hard words wear the soul; fortress and laugh
english: … longs for death, for the reasons stated above. But as to the inner sense he speaks mysteries: he reflects on things that have already happened and gives full assurance about what is to come. Such are always the sayings of the holy prophets. Now that we have come to the words themselves, let us make their sense clear, with him guiding our steps toward the interpretation who also strengthened holy Job for his contests.

“After this Job opened his mouth” (Job 3:1). Since it is a righteous man who opens his mouth, it is not fitting to attend to what is said just casually; we should search out the benefit that comes from the words. For such sayings of the saints are always full of benefit, and when a righteous man opens his mouth, he brings hidden treasures out into public. That is why Paul too, the chosen vessel, says in his letter: “My mouth is open to you, Corinthians” (2 Corinthians 6:11). And of the Lord it is written: “Opening his mouth, he taught” (Matthew 5:2). In short, the one who is attested as opening his mouth is the one who has first been taught the measures of silence. So Job too opens his mouth “after this”: that is, after the great trophy, after those sufferings. He does not speak without weighing his words, in anguish of body, with his tongue running ahead of the lawful rule of good sense; rather, even in his words he shows himself self-controlled. And the testimony that he “opened his mouth” shows both the calm of his soul and the fitness of his words.

“How long will you make my soul weary?” (Job 19:2). Just as heavy loads laid on the bodies of animals make the beasts that carry them weary, so there are some heavy words, and whoever hears them grows weary. As if pressed down by a weight — the force of the words spoken not [well], but harshly or in abuse, by the other two who had come with Baldad, like the feeling of a heavy load — Job, weary in soul at what they had said, says: “How long will you make my soul weary?”

And a little later: You see how the sovereign of the Sauchaeans was described beforehand. His words are tyrannical, and when Job hears them he says: “How long will you make my soul weary?” Nothing reaches a man's soul as a hard word does. Often someone who has endured tortures applied to his body has not endured words. The perfect athlete, though, even when he is weary, still endures harsh words; for to endure insult belongs to a great man. That is why the Apostle, among his own deeds of courage, says: “Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we bear it; being slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, until now” (1 Corinthians 4:12-13).

And a little later, on the words “How long will you make my soul weary?”, he says next: Do you see? It is Job, whose book contains nothing so especially as his courage and his endurance. And yet he feels the weariness he had suffered from the hard word of those who had come to visit him.

“Only know that the Lord has done this to me” (Job 19:3). What you see in my case, do not think it has come to me from anywhere but from God. Be afraid, then; for he who brings these things on me can bring them on you as well. “You speak against me; without shame before me you press upon me” (Job 19:3). Often a person even speaks against another and does wrong in it. But when he feels no shame, he says it to the other man's face, not to correct him or to tell the truth, but to reproach and insult him. For one must not trample on those who are being punished by God, but lament and be afraid.

“Yes, truly I have gone astray, and a deceiver lodges with me, so that I speak a word I ought not” (Job 19:4). Then he speaks by way of supposition: I grant you, as you assume, that I suffer these things because of my sins; ought you then to reproach me like this? “And a deceiver lodges with me.” Even if, for argument's sake, I had done such things as I ought not, even if I was that kind of man, ought you not, seeing the scourges, the running sores, the worms, the loss of my possessions, to have felt some respect? Instead you trample on me further, with no pity for me and no sympathy for my plight.

“But let it be that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach” (Job 19:5). You reproach me beyond measure; you leap on me, as if stepping on me and trampling me down, as you reproach me. “And he has raised his stronghold against me” (Job 19:6). It is as if I am under a wall: the stronghold of my plight, which I cannot escape until God decides to pull it down. “Behold, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak” (Job 19:7). This is the saying: “Overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
From the same: Look, at your reproach I am thought to laugh, not to speak.
